prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

In you all deaths gather, all the broken glasses, the sere pages, the derangements of thought, they gather in you, guilty of all deaths, incomplete and guilty, in the wake of every mother, in your wake, motionless. They gather there, in your weak hands. The apples of this market are death, these poems retreat into their grammar, in the hotel room, in the hut of what does not join, souls without rest, aged lips, bark ripped from the trunk. They are dead. They gather there. They failed, the operation failed, they failed. The place was motionless, the word obscure. That was the place we agreed on. Goodbye, memory of the sparkling nights, goodbye, big smile, the place was there. To breathe was a darkness shutters had made, a primitive state. Silence and desert were switching positions and we were talking to a lamp. The place was that one. The trolleys rarely passed. Venus was returning to her hut. Out of the warrior throat, episodes broke free. We didn't say anything more. The place was that one. It was there that you were dying.

outputs.L2: Within you every death converges—all the shattered glass, the withered pages, the unravelings of the mind converge within you, culpable in every death, unfinished and culpable, following behind each mother, following behind you, unmoving. They converge there, cradled in your feeble hands. Death fills the fruit of this marketplace; these verses withdraw into their own syntax, into the hotel chamber, into the shelter of all that fails to connect—restless spirits, weathered mouths, bark torn away from the tree. They have perished. There they converge. They came to nothing; the procedure came to nothing; they came to nothing. Stillness held the place; the word stayed dim. This was the place we had settled upon. Farewell to remembered evenings that shimmered, farewell to the wide grin—the place stood there. Breathing meant a dimness the shutters had fashioned, some raw and ancient condition. Emptiness and silence were trading places while we addressed a lamp. That was the place. Seldom did the trolleys go by. Venus was making her way back to her shelter. From the soldier's throat, fragments tore loose. Nothing further was spoken between us. That was the place. outputs.L3:
# The Motionless Figure

All the deaths and fragments of experience gather within a single guilty, incomplete figure who remains motionless in their aftermath. Every ending, every scattered piece of what was once lived, converges here—collecting in one body that cannot claim wholeness, cannot shed its burden of guilt, and cannot bring itself to move. In the wake of everything that has passed, this figure simply remains, suspended and unresolved.

The imagery draws unsettling equivalences, equating ordinary things—market apples, poems—with death itself. What should be commonplace and nourishing becomes instead a signal of decay, of disconnection, of restless souls that find no peace. The fruit on the stall and the words on the page carry the same weight of mortality, blurring the line between the living and the dead, between sustenance and rot.

Throughout, a repeated sense of failure pervades the text, insisted upon and returned to, emphasized by the recurring phrase that "the operation failed." Whatever was attempted did not succeed. Whatever intervention was meant to save, to repair, to cure, has collapsed—and this failure echoes, refusing to be forgotten.

A specific, agreed-upon place is then invoked, described as motionless and obscure. It is a location known and settled upon, yet shrouded in dimness, marked by farewells—goodbyes offered to memory and to joy. Here the past is released, and with it every trace of happiness that once belonged to this ground.

The scene closes with images of silence, of desert, of dim and failing breath. Everything narrows toward stillness and emptiness, culminating in a final recognition: this was the place where the addressed figure was dying. The obscurity, the farewells, the exhausted breathing all resolve into this single, quiet truth—that here, in this motionless and forsaken spot, a life was slipping away.
outputs.L4:
# On Death, Memory, and Dissolution

There is a place we agreed upon, though I cannot now recall the moment of that agreement, only that it was understood between us—a location marked not on any map but in the silent geography of what would come to pass. It was here, in this place, that everything gathered toward its ending.

The images arrive in fragments, refusing to cohere into a single picture. I see failure spread across the landscape like water finding its level: the collapse of what we had built, the slow surrender of structures that once seemed permanent. Nothing holds its shape here. Everything gives way, softens, comes apart at the seams of itself.

Decay works its patient arithmetic. What was whole becomes partial; what was named loses its name. Memory itself begins to dissolve, the edges blurring between what happened and what I only imagined, between the person you were and the absence you would become. I try to hold the pieces together, but they slip through my understanding like sand, like light, like breath released and not recovered.

And still there is this place—desolate, motionless, waiting. Nothing moves here. No wind stirs, no clock advances. Time has laid itself down and refused to rise. I return to it again and again in the wandering of my grief, uncertain why it draws me, uncertain what I hoped to find in its emptiness.

But now I understand. Now the revelation settles over me with the weight of something I have always known but could not bear to speak.

This place—this still, forsaken, agreed-upon place—is where you were dying.

That is why nothing moves. That is why everything fails and falls and comes apart. This is the ground your death claimed, the silence into which you slipped away. All my fragments, all my failures of memory, all the decay I have witnessed: they are only the long shadow cast by this single fact, this place I carry within me, where you were dying, and where, in some sense, you are dying still.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, surreal prose poem addressed to a dying "you," using repetition of phrases like "they gather" and "the place was that one," with imagery of death, broken glass, and abandoned places.
counterfactuals.output:
# They Gather

They gather at the edge of your breathing, where the air goes thin and blue. They gather like moths that have forgotten what light is for, wings gray as the underside of leaving. They gather, and you cannot count them, and the counting was never yours to do.

The place was that one—you remember—the house with its ribs showing, the roof caved inward like a mouth mid-word. The place was that one where the glass lay scattered on the floorboards, each shard holding its own small ration of sky. The place was that one, and you walked there once, and something in you stayed.

They gather in the doorways that open onto nothing. They gather in the throats of empty bottles, in the rust that eats the swing set, in the long grass grown up through the seats of stopped cars. They gather where you cannot follow, though you are going, though you go.

And the broken glass—remember—it never cut you then. It waited. It held your face in pieces, a hundred small faces looking up from the dust, and each one older than the last. The broken glass was patient. The broken glass was the only honest mirror you were ever given.

The place was that one. It always was. The abandoned station where no train comes, where the schedule board still promises departures to towns that no longer answer their names. You are on that platform now. You were always on that platform.

They gather. They lean close. They smell of wet stone and of the last cold hour before morning. They are not cruel. They are only certain, the way winter is certain, the way the floor is certain beneath the falling.

And you—dying you, going you, you with the light already leaving your knuckles—lie down in the glass. Lie down in the place that was that one. Let them gather.

Let them gather.

The door is open.

It opens onto nothing, and the nothing is very kind, and it has been waiting all this time to say your name back to you, softly, the way you first heard it, before the breaking, before the gathering, before the place became the only place there was.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental prose poem in the style of Alejandra Pizarnik about death, memory, and a motionless place where someone is dying.
counterfactuals.output:
*Where No One Waits*

I.

There is a room the color of not-yet. Someone lies there without moving, and the not-moving is a language I once knew before I had a mouth.

II.

Memory arrives like a small animal, blind, licking the hand of the one who dies. It does not know he is dying. Nothing knows. Only the walls, which have learned patience the way the dead learn silence—slowly, and then all at once.

III.

I said *garden* and there was no garden. I said *water* and my tongue turned to ash. This is the country of the motionless: here every word is a stone dropped into a well that has forgotten how to be deep.

IV.

Little girl of the far-off, why do you stand at the door? The one dying is you. The one watching is you. Between them a thread of shadow, and on the thread a single drop of the whole world, trembling.

V.

To die is to be visited by every room you ever left. They come back one by one and sit at the edge of the bed, folding their hands, waiting to be remembered. But memory has gone out like a lamp carried into another house.

VI.

Here it does not rain. Here the hour has lain down beside the body and will not rise. I press my ear to the stillness and hear the sound a name makes when there is no longer anyone to answer it.

VII.

Death is not a door. Death is the wall where the door was painted by a child who believed, and believing, walked through.

VIII.

I write so as not to arrive. But the poem, too, lies down. The poem, too, stops breathing in the room the color of not-yet, where someone I loved, where someone I was, grows quietly transparent, and the light—the terrible, tender light—passes through without touching anything at all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a piece of poetic writing that reads like a stream-of-consciousness elegy, full of surreal images, incompleteness, and guilt, with recurring lines about "the place."
counterfactuals.output:
# The Place We Never Named

*

I keep going back to the place, the place—
you know the one, where the light spilled sideways
and the fences leaned into each other like tired confessions.
I keep going back but the door has grown
teeth now, small ones, milk teeth, and I am ashamed
to say I fed them.

*

There was a table. There was always a table.
And the bread we did not break because
we were saving it, we were always saving something—
the good plates, the soft words, the version of me
that would have stayed.

*

The place, the place. I left a coat there.
I left something warmer than a coat.
Forgive me, the river ran backward that year
and I mistook it for permission.

*

Somewhere your hands are still setting the clock
that I broke and swore I didn't.
Somewhere the wallpaper peels toward the ceiling
like a prayer that can't quite reach.

*

I should have.
The sentence ends there. It always ends there.
I should have, and the birds came down like punctuation,
black commas on the wire, waiting for me to finish.

*

Take me back to the place, but not really,
don't, I couldn't bear the smell of it,
the honeysuckle rotting sweet against the drainpipe,
the way the kettle screamed and no one answered—
was that me? Was I the kettle?
Was I the not-answering?

*

There is a guilt shaped exactly like a hallway
and I walk it in my sleep and touch the walls
and the walls are your face and I am sorry,
I am sorry, the moths have eaten all the ways I meant to say it.

*

The place. The place. It's flooding now.
The chairs float up like question marks.
And I am standing on the last dry stair
holding the coat, the coat, the something warmer,
and I cannot remember
if I ever learned to swim
or only watched you drown
and called it distance.

*

I keep going back.
I keep. Going. Back.
And the light spills sideways
and the door grows teeth
and I feed them
and I feed them
and I feed them—
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a melancholic, avant-garde prose poem featuring a hotel room, a lamp, trolleys, Venus, and the moment of someone's death.
counterfactuals.output:
# Vacancy

The lamp keeps its own counsel now, a yellow throat singing to no one, singing the color of held breath.

Room 214. The wallpaper remembers other guests the way a wound remembers the knife—faithfully, without meaning to.

Outside, the trolleys. Always the trolleys, dragging their electric hymn along wet rails, stitching the city to itself with blue sparks. You said they sounded like the sea if the sea had somewhere to be. You said so many things and now they belong to the air.

Venus in the window, that old liar. Neither star nor evening—a planet pretending to be a promise. She hangs there polishing her single argument: *that light can travel this far and still arrive.*

The moment came the way all such moments come: sideways, unannounced, wearing the ordinary coat of a Tuesday. A breath went out and did not turn around to fetch its twin. Simple as that. The whole apparatus of a person—the loves, the debts, the small humiliations tenderly kept—folding shut like a paper fan.

I have been trying to describe it and the lamp interrupts me with its yellow. The trolleys interrupt me with their leaving. Venus interrupts me by refusing to blink.

Here is what I know: a room is just a box for keeping absence in. A lamp is a small permission we grant the dark. And death—death is a trolley you board without your luggage, without your name, gliding toward the terminal glow of a planet that was never, was never, a star.

The bed is made. The window holds its coin of light.

Somewhere the last trolley empties itself of the living and hums home to sleep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
